title: Grüezi — the word you cannot skip
text:
You greet BEFORE anything else. Walking into a shop and saying what you want, with no Grüezi in front of it, is what badly brought up people do.

• **Grüezi** to one person you do not know
• **Grüezi mitenand** to two or more
• **Hoi** or **Sali** to a friend, never to a stranger
• **Ade** on the way out

And you greet people you will never speak to again. The lift, the waiting room, a narrow pavement. Not saying it is noticed, and nobody will ever mention it.

**merci** is ordinary German here, not a French word borrowed for the occasion. Danke is correct and you will hear it far less.

title: Der, die, das — three words for "the"
text:
Every German noun carries a gender, and it is not about the thing.

• **der** Mann, **der** Zug, **der** See, **der** Berg
• **die** Frau, **die** Strasse, **die** Uhr, **die** Nacht
• **das** Haus, **das** Wasser, **das** Brot, **das** Kind

Das Mädchen is neuter. There is no logic to find, so do not look for one.

**Learn the article welded to the word.** Not "Zug, masculine" but "der Zug", one lump, the way you learned your own first words. Every entry in this course states it, and it costs nothing now and everything later.

title: The verb comes second. Always second.
text:
German will move almost anything to the front of a sentence, and the verb stays in second place regardless. Whatever got moved, the subject goes behind the verb to make room.

• Ich **gehe** heute in die Stadt.
• Heute **gehe** ich in die Stadt.
• In die Stadt **gehe** ich heute.

All three are correct and they emphasise different things. What is never correct is *Heute ich gehe*, which is the one an English speaker reaches for first.

Second **position**, not second word. "Der alte Mann" is one position.

title: Verbs that come apart
text:
Some verbs have a front half that detaches and goes to the end of the sentence. You have been reading it happen for sixteen stories.

• ankommen → Der Zug **kommt** in Luzern **an**.
• aussteigen → Ich **steige** langsam **aus**.
• mitkommen → **Kommen** Sie **mit**.

The longer the sentence, the further apart they get, and the meaning is not finished until that last word lands. This is why Germans seem to be waiting for the end of your sentence. They are.

You do not have to learn a list. You have to notice the stray little word at the end and put it back on the front.

title: kein or nicht
text:
Two ways to say no, and they are not interchangeable.

**kein** cancels a noun. It replaces ein.
• Ich habe **keinen** Schirm.
• Es gibt **kein** Brot mehr.

**nicht** cancels everything else — a verb, an adjective, a whole sentence.
• Ich verstehe **nicht**.
• Der Laden ist **nicht** offen.

The test: if the thing you are cancelling could have had *ein* in front of it, use kein.

title: Sie and du
text:
Two ways of saying "you", and picking wrong is louder than a grammar mistake.

**Sie** — a stranger, anybody older, a shopkeeper, an official. Capital S, always. *Kommen Sie mit. Wo wohnen Sie?*

**du** — friends, people your own age once you know them, children, family. *Kommst du mit? Wo wohnst du?*

You start with Sie and you wait. The other person offers du when they are ready, and in Switzerland that can take a while — being offered it is a small event, not a formality.

Being too formal costs nothing. Being too familiar with somebody who is seventy costs a surprising amount.

title: Franken, Rappen and the .95
text:
One franc is a hundred Rappen, and nothing smaller than five Rappen exists any more.

• **4.50** is said *vier Franken fünfzig*, or just *vier fünfzig*
• **3.95** is *drei Franken fünfundneunzig*

Prices ending .95 are everywhere and they are doing the same job as .99 anywhere else.

Cash still works everywhere and nobody thinks twice about it. What does get noticed is handing over a fifty for a four-franc coffee. Break your notes when you get the chance.

title: halb acht is half past SEVEN
text:
The one that catches every English speaker, and it catches them at a station.

German counts **towards** the coming hour, not away from the one just gone.

• **halb acht** = 7:30, half way to eight
• **Viertel vor acht** = 7:45
• **Viertel nach acht** = 8:15

A timetable will say *acht Uhr dreissig* and be perfectly clear. A person will say *halb acht* and mean the same moment.

**Punkt acht** means eight exactly, and here that is not a figure of speech.

title: The Swiss word, not the German one
text:
Some everyday things simply have a different name here, and using the German German one marks you out faster than an accent does.

• **Billett**, not Fahrkarte
• **Perron**, not Bahnsteig
• **Gipfeli**, not Hörnchen
• **Weggli**, not Brötchen
• **Sack**, not Tüte
• **Spital**, not Krankenhaus
• **Velo**, not Fahrrad

A lot of them came in through French, which is why so many look like it. They are not slang and they are not dialect. They are what the newspaper prints.

And there is no **ß** in Switzerland at all. Strasse, gross, heisst. Ever.

title: Long words are short words stuck together
text:
German glues nouns end to end and calls the result one word. This looks like the hardest thing about the language and it is one of the easiest.

• Bahn + Hof = **Bahnhof**, the train yard
• Flug + Hafen = **Flughafen**, the flight harbour
• Fahr + Plan = **Fahrplan**, the going plan
• Trink + Wasser = **Trinkwasser**

**The last piece is the word.** A Fahrplan is a plan. A Rolltreppe is a staircase. Everything in front of it is a description.

So you never have to be taught Vierwaldstättersee. Four, forest places, lake. It is a lake.

title: müssen, dürfen, können — and the verb that gets sent to the end
text:
Five little verbs, and the whole Hausordnung is written out of three of them.

• **müssen** — you have to. *Ich muss die Miete bezahlen.*
• **dürfen** — you are allowed to. *Man darf nach zehn nicht duschen.*
• **können** — you are able to. *Ich kann selber putzen.*
• **wollen** — you want to. *Ich will keine Probleme.*
• **sollen** — you are supposed to. *Man soll die Treppe putzen.*

**The real verb goes to the END of the clause, and it goes there as an infinitive.** *Ich muss die Wohnung sehr gut **putzen**.* Everything else piles up in the middle and the meaning does not finish until that last word lands.

You have seen this bracket before: it is the same one a separable verb makes. German opens something at position two and closes it at the end, and once you hear the opening you are waiting for the close.

**darf nicht is a prohibition, muss nicht is not.** *Du darfst nicht* means you may not. *Du musst nicht* means you do not have to.

title: der becomes den, and nothing else moves
text:
A German noun changes with its job in the sentence. The first change worth learning is the accusative — the thing the verb is done TO.

**And it is smaller than it looks. Only the masculine moves.**

• der Tisch → Ich nehme **den** Tisch.
• ein Stuhl → Ich kaufe **einen** Stuhl.
• kein Velo → Ich habe **kein** Velo. *(neuter, unchanged)*
• die Wohnung → Ich putze **die** Wohnung. *(feminine, unchanged)*
• das Bad → Ich sehe **das** Bad. *(neuter, unchanged)*

Three of the four do nothing at all. Learn **der → den** and **ein → einen** and you have most of it.

This is why the article has to be learned welded to the noun. If you do not know a Tisch is *der*, you cannot know it becomes *den* — and that is the mistake that never goes away on its own.

title: man — the word every rule is written in
text:
**man** is not *ein Mann*. It means people-in-general, the way English says "you" without meaning you personally.

• *Man darf hier nicht rauchen.* — no smoking here.
• *Man muss sich eintragen.* — you have to sign up.
• *Das macht man so.* — that is how it is done.

It takes the same verb form as *er*: man **darf**, man **muss**, man **macht**.

**Every rule in this country is written with it.** The Hausordnung, the signs at the Sammelstelle, the notice in the Waschküche. Nobody is being told off and nobody is named — the rule simply exists and applies to everybody. That is very Swiss, and once you hear it you hear it everywhere.

title: seit — where German uses the present and English does not
text:
Something that started in the past and is STILL GOING takes the **present tense** in German. English insists on a past form here, and that mismatch is one of the commonest mistakes learners make in both directions.

• *Ich wohne seit einem Monat hier.* — I **have been** living here a month.
• *Er arbeitet seit elf Jahren dort.* — he **has** worked there eleven years.
• *Sie wohnt seit vierzig Jahren im gleichen Haus.*

Say *ich habe gewohnt* and a German speaker understands that you have stopped.

**seit takes the dative**, which is why it is *seit einem Monat* and not *seit ein Monat*. That is worth noticing now and not worrying about yet.

title: The shoes come off. Nobody will ask you.
text:
You take your shoes off at the door. Your own flat, somebody else’s flat, it makes no difference.

**Nobody asks and nobody offers.** The caretaker does it. The men delivering your furniture do it. The neighbour coming up to complain about the noise does it — he climbs two floors in his socks to knock on your door.

There is no sentence for this. There is a small pile of shoes by every front door and you add yours to it.

Keeping them on is not rude in a loud way. It is the sort of thing nobody mentions and everybody notices, which is the most Swiss category of mistake there is.

title: Four bins, and one of them costs money
text:
Everything gets separated, and it is not only about the environment.

• **Glas** → the Sammelstelle, sorted by colour: white, brown, green
• **PET** and **Alu** → back to the shop
• **Papier** and **Karton** → out on the street, flat and tied with string, on their own day
• **Kehricht** → the Gebührensack, and only that bag

**Here is the part that explains the rest.** Glass, paper and PET cost nothing. The Kehricht costs, because you pay for its collection in the price of the bag — over two francs a bag. Anybody with a lot of rubbish pays a lot.

So separating carefully is not virtue, it is arithmetic. That is why everybody does it, and why the wrong bag gets opened, looked into, and left on the pavement with a sticker on it.

title: Everything is an Abo, and every Abo has a Frist
text:
The phone, the train, the gym, the newspaper, the insurance. All of it is an **Abo** and all of it renews itself.

Two words decide everything, and they are the two to find before you sign:

• **die Dauer** — how long it runs. Twenty-four months is normal.
• **die Frist** — how long before the end you have to give notice. Three months is normal.

**kündigen** is the verb. Not cancelling — giving notice, in writing, in time. Miss the Frist by a day and it runs another year.

A phone for one franc is not a phone for one franc. It is a phone paid for in twenty-four small pieces, and that is in the contract, which is why reading it matters more here than the price does.

title: Bills come on paper, and they have a deadline
text:
Not by email. On paper, into the letterbox, with a QR code in the bottom right corner.

Everything is in that code — the account, the amount, your name. Hold your phone over it, or put the bill into the machine at the post office, or queue at the counter and pay in cash. All three are normal.

**Three words to read first:**
• **der Betrag** — the amount
• **das Datum** — the deadline, usually thirty days
• **die Mahnung** — what arrives if you miss it, and it costs twenty francs

The habit everybody here has: the bill comes, you pay it the same day, it goes in the folder. Not because anybody is virtuous, but because a Mahnung is expensive and a second one is worse.

title: The past everybody actually speaks
text:
German has a written past and a spoken past, and outside a book you will hear the spoken one almost every time.

It is two pieces. **haben** in second position, and the verb itself, changed, parked at the end.

• Ich **habe** einen Kaffee **getrunken**.
• Sie **hat** nichts **gesagt**.
• Wir **haben** zwei Stunden **geredet**.

The piece at the end is the participle. Regular verbs build it with **ge...t**: sagen becomes gesagt, machen gemacht, kaufen gekauft. Strong verbs use **ge...en** and often change the vowel: trinken becomes getrunken, sprechen gesprochen, nehmen genommen. There is no rule for the vowel, so the course states it on every verb card.

The bracket is the same one the modals taught you. Ich **muss** den Sack **spülen**, ich **habe** den Sack **gespült**. Something is in second place, something is at the end, and everything else lives in between.

title: Some verbs take bin, not habe
text:
A short list of verbs builds the same past with **sein** instead of haben.

• Ich **bin** nach Hause **gegangen**.
• Er **ist** um sieben **gekommen**.
• Wir **sind** zwei Stunden **gefahren**.

They are the verbs of going somewhere and of becoming something else: gehen, kommen, fahren, laufen, steigen, fallen, and also bleiben, sein and werden, which do not move at all and take sein anyway.

**Here is the Swiss part.** Standing, sitting and lying take **sein** in Switzerland and in the south generally, and **haben** in the north.

• Ich **bin** am Fenster **gestanden**.
• Wir **sind** am Tisch **gesessen**.

In Hamburg that would be ich habe gestanden. Both are correct German. This course says bin, because this course is in Luzern.

title: The third case, and who gets it
text:
When something is handed over, two things are in the sentence: the thing, and the person who gets it. The person goes in the **dative**.

• Er gibt **mir** das Messer.
• Ich gebe **ihm** das Brett zurück.
• Sie gibt **uns** zwei Teller.

The whole list, and it is short: **mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen**, and **Ihnen** for the polite Sie.

The articles change too: der becomes **dem**, das becomes **dem**, die becomes **der**, and in the plural die becomes **den** with an **n** added to the noun.

• mit **dem** Zug, in **der** Küche, bei **den** Nachbarn

**mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus** always take it, with no thinking required. Seit **einem** Monat. Nach **dem** Essen. Bei **der** Post.

title: Verbs that hand you the dative
text:
A handful of very common verbs put their person in the dative even though English feels like it should be an object.

• Er hilft **mir**. Not: er hilft mich.
• Das gehört **ihr**.
• Die Stadt gefällt **mir**.
• Der Käse schmeckt **ihm**.

The ones you will meet first: **helfen, gehören, gefallen, schmecken, passen, danken, begegnen, gratulieren**.

**gefallen** is worth a second look, because it turns the sentence round. Not I like the town, but the town pleases me. The thing is the subject and does the work, and you sit in the dative and receive it.

• Die Stadt **gefällt mir**.
• Die Preise **gefallen mir** nicht.

And **es tut mir leid** is the same shape. The sorrow does the acting, and it does it to you.

title: Wollen wir du sagen?
text:
Phase 0 said: start with Sie and wait. This is what the waiting ends with.

**You never switch on your own.** The older or more senior person offers it, and the offer is a small ceremony: their first name, your hand, your first name.

• **Wollen wir du sagen?**

That is the sentence. Yes is very nearly the only answer, and it is permanent. A du never goes back to Sie, which is exactly why people think about it for weeks before they offer one.

Two verbs cover the act itself. **duzen** is to say du, **siezen** is to say Sie.

• Wir **duzen** uns.
• Er **siezt** mich immer noch.

**Where du is automatic:** in a club, in sport, and on a mountain path. A man of seventy says du to a child on a hiking trail and Sie to the same child in town, and nobody finds that strange.

Expect to get it wrong for about three weeks. The mouth keeps saying Sie after the agreement, and everybody who has done this knows it.

title: mal, and the invitation that is not one
text:
**mal** is a tiny word that softens whatever it lands on. Schau **mal**. Komm **mal** vorbei. Wir sollten **mal** essen gehen.

It is friendly, and it is not a plan.

• **Wir sollten mal einen Kaffee trinken.** Nothing will happen.
• **Hast du am Dienstag Zeit?** Something will happen.

The difference is a date. Plans here are made in calendars, three weeks ahead, and once a day and a time exist the thing is fixed. Nobody cancels the week of. Nobody forgets.

So waiting for a message after a sentence with mal in it is waiting for a train that is not on the timetable. This is not a lie, and the person meant the friendly thing they said. If you want the meal, **you** name the day. That takes more nerve and it works.

title: Saying yes at the local volume
text:
Enthusiasm is expressed quietly here, and **gern** does most of the work.

• **Ja, gern.** A full yes.
• **Sehr gern.** More than a full yes.
• **Klar.** An easy yes.
• **Ja, wieso nicht.** Half a yes, and still a yes.

A gern is worth as much as a grossartig somewhere else. You only have to convert the size. Answering an ordinary invitation with oh, das ist wunderbar, sehr sehr gern lands about three sizes too big, and the room quietly puts it back down.

For no, the word is **leider**.

• **Das geht leider nicht.**
• **Ich habe leider schon etwas abgemacht.**

Give a short reason or none at all. Nobody asks what. And **keine Lust** is a real answer that nobody takes badly, which is better than yes now and a cancellation later.

title: Adjectives in front of the noun
text:
After the verb an adjective never changes. **Der Stuhl ist alt.** Nothing added, nothing to learn.

In front of the noun it always changes.

• **der alte** Stuhl, **ein alter** Stuhl
• **die alte** Lampe, **eine alte** Lampe
• **das alte** Buch, **ein altes** Buch

The ending depends on what stands in front. When the article already shows the gender, the adjective coasts on **e** or **en**. When it does not, the adjective has to carry it instead, which is why ein **alter** Stuhl and das **alte** Buch look so different.

**Nobody learns this from the table.** You hear it a few hundred times and the wrong one starts to sound wrong, which is the only way anybody has ever learned it, native speakers included. The table is for checking afterwards, not for building sentences from.

title: Komm. Geh. Zieh das an.
text:
To tell somebody to do something, take the du form and drop the du and the **st**.

• du kommst, **komm**
• du gehst, **geh**
• du bringst, **bring**

It sounds short and it is not unfriendly. **Komm essen** is two words and a whole invitation.

For Sie, keep the verb and add Sie: **Kommen Sie. Setzen Sie sich.**

A verb with a front piece leaves it at the end, in an order too.

• **Zieh** die Jacke **an**.
• **Zieh** die Schuhe **aus**.
• **Mach** das Licht **an**.

And the reflexive ones keep their little word: **Setz dich.** **Setzen Sie sich.** The person doing the sitting is also the person being sat, and German makes you say so.

title: Nine words that take both cases
text:
Most prepositions pick a case and keep it. **mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus** are always dative. **für, ohne, gegen, um** are always accusative.

Nine of them do not pick. They take **whichever case answers the question you are asking**.

• **in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen**

**Wo? Dative.** Where the thing already is.

• Ich sitze **auf dem** Stuhl.
• Das Velo steht **neben der** Post.
• Wir sind **auf dem** See.

**Wohin? Accusative.** Where the thing is going.

• Ich setze mich **auf den** Stuhl.
• Ich stelle das Velo **neben die** Post.
• Wir fahren **auf den** See hinaus.

The verb usually gives it away. **stehen, liegen, sitzen, sein** are places, so dative. **stellen, legen, setzen, gehen, fahren** are movements, so accusative.

And the movement has to be INTO the thing you named. *Ich gehe in der Stadt spazieren* is dative, because the walking happens inside the town rather than into it.

title: hin goes away, her comes towards
text:
German marks the direction of travel relative to the speaker, and it does it with two little pieces.

**hin** is away from me. **her** is towards me.

• Ich gehe **hinauf**. (I am going up, away from where I am now)
• Komm **herauf**! (Come up, to where I am)

They stick to the front of a direction word and to the back of a verb.

• **hinauf, hinunter, hinein, hinaus, hinüber**
• Er ist **hingegangen**. Sie ist **hinaufgelaufen**.

Up a mountain you will hear all of them in an afternoon. **Wir fahren hinauf**, **wir gehen hinunter**, **er kommt herunter**, **das Schiff fährt hinaus**.

And **wohin** and **woher** are the same two pieces with a question on the front. Where to, where from.

title: What people actually say
text:
Nobody says hinunter out loud. In speech every one of those words loses its front half.

| written | spoken |
|---|---|
| hinauf | **rauf** |
| hinunter | **runter** |
| hinein | **rein** |
| hinaus | **raus** |
| hinüber | **rüber** |

• **Komm rein.**
• **Geh raus.**
• **Wir fahren runter.**

The short form has quietly lost the hin and her distinction as well, so **rauf** does the work of both hinauf and herauf and nobody minds.

Write the long one. Say the short one. Reading a text out loud and hearing runter where the page says hinunter is the moment this stops being two lists and starts being one word.

title: grösser, teurer, schneller
text:
To compare, put **er** on the end and **als** after it.

• Zürich ist **grösser als** Luzern.
• Das Schiff ist **schneller als** der Zug.
• Die Rigi ist **runder** und **breiter**.

Short adjectives usually take an umlaut with the er: **alt/älter, gross/grösser, jung/jünger, lang/länger, hoch/höher, warm/wärmer**.

Four do their own thing and you simply have to know them.

• gut, **besser**, am **besten**
• viel, **mehr**, am **meisten**
• gern, **lieber**, am **liebsten**
• hoch, **höher**, am **höchsten**

For the top of the scale it is **am ...sten**: am grössten, am teuersten, am schnellsten.

And **so ... wie** is for things that are equal. **Die Glocke ist so gross wie ein Kopf.**

title: gern, lieber, am liebsten
text:
There is no verb for to prefer. The whole job is done by one adverb in three sizes.

• Ich trinke **gern** Tee. (I like tea)
• Ich trinke **lieber** Tee. (I would rather have tea)
• Ich trinke **am liebsten** Tee. (Tea is my favourite)

It goes with the verb, not with the noun, so it works for anything you do.

• Ich gehe **lieber** zu Fuss.
• Ich fahre **am liebsten** mit dem Schiff.
• Ich sitze **lieber** unten.

**lieber** also softens a suggestion into something you can refuse. *Gehen wir lieber morgen?* is a proposal. *Gehen wir morgen* is a plan.

title: Four minutes is enough
text:
The whole network is built to connect, and once you see it the timetable stops being a list.

Trains arrive just before the hour and leave just after it. In between, everything is standing in the station at the same time. That is why a **four minute connection** is normal and why it works: the other train is at the same platform, waiting, on purpose.

• **die Verbindung** — the whole journey, however many trains it is
• **der Anschluss** — the next train after this one
• **abfahren, ankommen, umsteigen** — and all three park their front half at the end

One ticket covers all of it. Train, bus, boat, from A to B, and what runs in between is not your problem.

On the platform, read the **direction**, not the destination. The train to Stans says Engelberg on the board, because Stans is on the way and Engelberg is the end of the line.

And when it does go wrong, the loudspeaker names the next train before you can ask.

title: The signs give you a time, not a distance
text:
Every path has a yellow sign, and behind each place name is **a time**.

• Alpnachstad, **2 h 40**

Not kilometres. Two flat kilometres are twenty minutes and two steep ones are an hour, so the distance would tell you nothing.

The times are accurate to about the minute, for a normal person, with no breaks. If you take fifteen minutes longer you took a photograph, sat down twice and went the wrong way once.

**The colours mean something.**

• **yellow** — a path for anybody
• **white and red** — a mountain path, boots and a head for heights
• **blue** — snow and ice, and you need equipment

Sixty thousand kilometres of it, marked and maintained by a **club** rather than the state, by people who walk their own forty kilometres twice a year with a tin of paint.

title: The card everybody has
text:
**Das Halbtax** halves every fare in the country: train, bus, boat, most mountain railways. More than half the population owns one, and for anybody who travels twice a month it pays for itself inside two months.

It is a card with a bad photograph on it, and the photograph stays bad for three years.

**Carry it.** A ticket bought at the Halbtax price without the card in your pocket is not a valid ticket, and the difference is expensive.

**Das GA** is the next step up: everything, free, for a great deal of money a year. Worth it for a long commute and for nobody else.

And **gültig** is the word that governs all of it. A ticket is valid for a day, a Halbtax for a year, and a Kriens rubbish bag is not valid in Luzern.

title: dass, and the verb goes to the back
text:
You can speak German for a year without this. Phases 0 to 3 do: **Er hat gesagt: Sie kommt.** That works, and it sounds like a report.

With **dass** it sounds like a conversation, and one thing happens.

• Er hat gesagt: Du **läufst** anders.
• Er hat gesagt, dass du anders **läufst**.

**The verb goes to the very end.** Everything else stays where it was, and there is a comma before the dass.

• Ich weiss, dass du hier **bist**.
• Sie hat gesagt, dass sie **kommt**.
• Er denkt, dass es **regnet**.

**ob** does exactly the same and means whether.

• Ich weiss nicht, ob er **kommt**.
• Sie fragt, ob du am Sonntag **kommst**.

That is the whole rule, and once you hear it you will hear it fifty times a day. The pause before the dass is where the sentence turns round.

title: weil sends the verb away, denn does not
text:
Two words for because, and they build the sentence differently.

• Ich bleibe zu Hause, **denn** es **regnet**.
• Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** es **regnet**.

After **denn** nothing moves: it is just two sentences with a word between them. After **weil** the verb goes to the end, exactly like dass.

With a longer sentence the difference is obvious.

• ..., **denn** ich **habe** den Zug verpasst.
• ..., **weil** ich den Zug verpasst **habe**.

**Everything before this phase used denn**, on purpose, so that the verb could stay in second position while there was enough else to think about. Both are correct and people say both. **weil** is far commoner in speech.

**deshalb** and **darum** are the other direction: not because, but therefore, and they take the front of their own sentence with the verb straight after.

• Es hat geregnet, **deshalb sind** wir drinnen geblieben.

title: Saying what is wrong, in as few words as possible
text:
Feelings are talked about here, and briefly, and to one person rather than six.

**Reach for the smaller word first.** It is easier to say and it is usually the more honest one.

• **Ich bin unsicher.** — I do not know where I stand
• **Ich bin verletzt.** — that hurt
• **Ich bin eifersüchtig.** — the big one, and there is no nice version of it
• **Ich habe Angst, dass ...** — the sentence under most of the others

The form is one sentence and then a pause. Not a speech. **Man sagt ein Wort und wartet.**

**Say it on the second day, not the fourteenth.** On the second day it is small. After a fortnight it is a story with a shape, and the other person has to take the shape as well as the thing.

And the answer you are looking for is not reassurance. It is **ich weiss**, or a question back: *wegen ihm oder wegen mir?*

title: An apology has to name the thing
text:
Two sizes, and they are not interchangeable.

**Entschuldigung** is the small one: a foot, an elbow, a squeeze past on the bus. You will say it ten times a week and it means nothing much.

**Es tut mir leid** is for an actual mistake, and it is said rarely.

**And it has to be specific.** *Es tut mir leid* on its own reads as evasion, the way a general sorry does. Name the thing.

• Es tut mir leid **für die zwei Tage**.
• Es tut mir leid, **dass ich nichts gesagt habe**.

The biggest one is **ich war im Unrecht**. People go years without saying it.

**And the reply is not ist schon gut.** That would make it smaller, and the person went to some trouble to make it that size. The reply here is **ich weiss** — which takes the apology and lets it stand.

Then somebody says Kaffee, and that is the end of it.

title: Schatz, and the little li on the end
text:
**Schatz** means treasure, and it is the ordinary word for the person you live with. **Liebling** exists and sounds a generation older.

The rule is not which word. The rule is **where**. Indoors, alone: Schatz. At a table with other people: your name. Two words for the same person, one for outside and one for in.

**The li ending makes anything small and warm**, and it is Swiss to the bone.

• Schatz → **Schätzli**
• Bier → **Bierli**
• Moment → **Momentli**
• Kaffee → **Kafi**

Grown men say these all day and none of it is baby talk.

**And then there is the trap.** *Ein Freund* is a friend. *Mein Freund* is a boyfriend. *Ein Freund von mir* is a friend again. Say *meine Freundin* in an office and the whole floor knows by lunchtime, and nobody will have asked you a single question.

title: eigentlich, eher, an sich
text:
A handful of small words that make a sentence softer, and reverse it while they are there.

• **Das ist eigentlich gut.** — it is not entirely good
• **Er ist eher ruhig.** — he hardly ever talks
• **Das ist an sich richtig.** — but
• **Das ist vielleicht ein bisschen viel.** — that is too much

**The but never arrives.** It lives inside the eigentlich, and everybody at the table hears it.

This is how you are told something without being told it, and it is how an opinion about you travels. *Er ist eher still*, said to somebody else while you are in the room, is not gossip: it is the normal way an assessment is delivered here.

**Do not defend yourself against it.** *Wer sich verteidigt, hat schon verloren.* Say nothing, and the sentence stands or it does not.

And use them yourself. **Das ist eine gute Frage** and **da muss ich noch schauen** are complete, polite refusals to answer, and nobody asks twice.

title: The future is the present with a date on it
text:
German has a proper future with **werden**, and almost nobody uses it for the future.

• Ich **werde** nach Portugal **fahren**. — correct, and it sounds like a letter
• **Nächstes Jahr fahre** ich nach Portugal. — what people say

**The time word does the work.** Nächstes Jahr, ab Januar, im Sommer, am zwölften. Put one in front and the present tense becomes the future.

**werden** is kept for something else: when you are not sure.

• Es **wird wohl** regnen.
• Das **wird** nicht klappen.

Then it is not a future, it is a guess.

**And the far future is barely spoken at all.** A plan for the twelfth of March is normal; a sentence about ten years' time sounds like a decision already taken, for both of you. When it does come it comes sideways, in the present tense, in the middle of something else: *in fünf Jahren machen wir hier eine Wand weg*, said while cleaning a floor.

title: The scale under wie geht es
text:
**Wie geht es?** is a greeting with more words in it, and **gut, danke** is the greeting back. Nothing has been asked and nothing has been answered.

Underneath it there is a real scale, and everybody knows it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **sehr gut** | suspicious |
| **gut** | the normal answer, means nothing |
| **es geht** | it is not going particularly well |
| **nicht so gut** | something is up |
| **mies** | it is genuinely bad |

**es geht** is the one that matters. Two words, and it means: ask again if you want to. Somebody who says **gut** does not want to talk. Somebody who says **es geht** might.

So when you hear it, ask. **Was ist?** is enough, and it changes the afternoon.

And the answer to somebody's bad February is not *es wird besser*. It is **alle sind so** — everybody is like this right now, not just you. That is the whole medicine.

title: Seven francs forty
text:
Nobody here talks about money, with one exception: **between two people it is discussed in complete detail**, and the detail is the point.

After a day out somebody works it out and sends the difference. Seven francs forty. That is not meanness and it is not coldness.

**teilen** — everybody pays their share, so nobody owes anybody anything.

**schulden** is the word people are avoiding. *Ich schulde dir noch zwanzig Franken* is a small weight, and nobody wants to carry one, in money or in favours. Splitting to the franc is how you put it down.

**sich etwas leisten** is the other one you need.

• **Das kann ich mir nicht leisten.**

A completely normal sentence, said by people with money too, and nobody is embarrassed by it. At home you would say you were busy. Here you say it is too expensive, and the table takes the answer and moves on.

And between a couple the fair split is often **the same share of each income**, not the same number of francs.

title: Könntest du, and the four verbs that carry it
text:
Everything you have said so far has been direct. *Kannst du mir helfen?* is a perfectly good sentence and nobody minds it.

There is a softer set of forms, and here it is not decoration. **It is what leaves the other person room to say no.**

Four verbs carry almost all of it:

• **hätte** — Ich hätte eine Bitte.
• **wäre** — Wäre das möglich?
• **könnte** — Könntest du mir helfen?
• **würde** — Würdest du das anschauen?

Everything else goes with **würde** plus the plain verb at the end. *Ich würde gern etwas fragen.* You do not need a form for every verb.

**Kannst du** and **könntest du** ask for the same thing. The difference is that the second one has already accepted no as an answer.

An older person of Rosmarie's generation will spend four minutes getting to a request that takes you ten to do, and every one of those minutes is built out of these four verbs. Hearing them is the signal: **something is being asked, and you are being given a way out.**

title: Nobody will offer. Ask, and everybody says yes.
text:
This is the one that costs foreigners the most, and it is not about grammar.

**Nobody here asks whether you need help.** Not because they do not care. Asking would say *I can see you are not managing*, and that is the rude part. So they wait.

And the moment you ask, they all say yes, immediately, and bring a trailer you did not ask for.

How it is said:

• **Ich hätte eine Bitte.** — the opening. It warns that something is coming.
• **Könntest du mir am Samstag helfen?** — the thing itself, with a date.
• **Hättest du Zeit?** — softer still.

Say what it is, say when, and stop. Do not explain why you cannot do it alone. Nobody asked.

**bitten** is not **fragen**. Fragen wants an answer. Bitten wants somebody to do something. *Ich bitte dich um Hilfe.*

The payment for a move is food and drink, and it is not optional. Money would be an insult.

title: Two words and a hand
text:
There is a fixed formula, and it exists so that nobody has to invent one.

• **Herzliches Beileid.**
• **Mein Beileid.**
• **Herzliche Anteilnahme** — the written one, for a card or a notice.

You say it and you give your hand, and you hold it one second longer than usual. **The hand matters more than the words.**

It feels cold if you come from somewhere that expects a personal sentence. It is the opposite of cold. The person standing at the front of that church says the same two words back two hundred times in an afternoon; a formula is the only thing that lets them stay standing. And it means you cannot get it wrong.

What is not said:

• not *she had a good life*
• not *now she has it behind her*
• not *I know how you feel*
• and you do not ask what she died of. If the family wants that said, they say it.

One sentence you may add, **only if you mean it**: *Wenn ich etwas machen kann, sagen Sie es.* Somebody will come back to you on it.

title: Es wird gemacht, and nobody is named
text:
**werden** plus the verb at the end, and the person doing it disappears.

• Die Wohnung **wird** geräumt.
• Der Vertrag **wurde** gekündigt.
• Das Herz **wird** kontrolliert.

You will meet this in exactly two places, and they are the two places it matters: **at the doctor and in anything official.**

A doctor cannot say *ich mache das schon*. He can only say what is being done. That is not distance, it is honesty about who is in charge of what.

And an official letter is written this way from the first line to the last, because it is not one person writing to you. *Die Rechnung wird in vier Raten bezahlt.*

The past is **wurde**: *Sie wurde am Donnerstag geräumt.* One form, and you will read it far more often than you say it.

title: als for the moment, während for the stretch
text:
Three words that all mean *when*, and they are not interchangeable.

**als** — once, one moment, in the past.
*Als wir geheiratet haben, hat es geregnet.*

**wenn** — every time, or in the future.
*Wenn ich sie besuche, bringe ich die Zeitung mit.*

**wann** — only in a question.
*Wann kommst du?*

One moment in the past is **als**, always. It is the commonest mistake there is, and it never stops being wrong.

**während** is the long stretch: *Während er gearbeitet hat, war ich in der Wohnung.*

All four send the verb to the end. And when the sentence starts with one of them, the two verbs end up next to each other in the middle: *Als wir geheiratet haben, hat es geregnet.* That looks wrong and is right.

**damals** is not a clause at all, just a word for back-then, and old people use it constantly. Twelve times in one evening is normal.

title: A no is cheap here. An excuse is expensive.
text:
Where you come from, a bare no is rude, so you build a reason around it. Here that is exactly backwards.

An invented reason is checked. Not out of suspicion — out of the opposite. They assume it is true, so they remember it, and they come back to it a week later. Then you are the person who was not honest about a Tuesday.

The forms are short and they are finished:

• **Nein, das geht nicht.**
• **Leider nein.**
• **Ich kann leider nicht.**
• **Das liegt bei mir nicht drin.** — for something bigger, usually money.

No *aber* afterwards. And then **be quiet**. That is the hard part: whoever keeps talking after a no is taking it back.

The one thing worth adding is a **date**. *Im Mai geht es nicht. Komm im September.* A no without a date is a door. A no with a date is an appointment.

title: The doctor only has what you say
text:
You learnt this language for an office and a station. Not for this.

The whole job at a doctor's is **describing it**, and there are about fourteen sentences in the world for it:

• Es **sticht**. Es **drückt**. Es **brennt**. Es **zieht**.
• Es ist **scharf**. Es ist **dumpf**.
• Es **strahlt aus** — it goes down the leg or the arm.
• Es ist besser, wenn ich liege.
• Es ist schlimmer am Morgen.
• Ich habe seit fünf Wochen Schmerzen.

Learn those and you can walk into any practice in the country.

How the system works: you go to the **Hausarzt** first, always. He writes an **Überweisung** and sends you on. The same word is used for moving money, and that is not a coincidence — it means passing something along.

The waiting is real and it is sorted by need: whoever is genuinely ill is seen at once, and a back waits eight weeks. That is the right order, and you only notice it when you are the back.

title: Woher kommst du wirklich?
text:
Three ordinary words, and one question they ruin.

**eigentlich**, **wirklich** and **ursprünglich** are useful and normal. *Eigentlich wollte ich früher gehen. Das ist wirklich gut. Ursprünglich war das ein Bauernhaus.*

Put any of them into *woher kommst du* and they all do the same thing: **they say your first answer was not the right one.**

For you this stops. In ten years you will sound like everybody else and nobody will ask. For somebody born here with a name from somewhere else, it does not stop, ever — and that is the part worth understanding before you ask anybody anything.

The people who ask are usually kind and mean nothing by it. That is what makes it hard to say anything about.

If you are asked, the short answer is fine and it is the true one: **Von hier.** *Ich wohne in Luzern.* You do not owe a biography to a stranger at a table.

title: Das liegt nicht drin
text:
Money is the thing nobody here talks about. You will not learn what a colleague earns in ten years, and you will not see who has little: the clothes are clean and the car is twelve years old either way.

So there is a sentence for it that does not use the word money:

• **Das liegt nicht drin.** — that is not possible, there is no room for it.

*Dieses Jahr liegt kein Skilager drin.* Everybody understands, nobody asks why, and the table moves on. That silence is the politeness.

The three that arrive together and catch everybody once:

• the **Depot** on a new flat — three months' rent, locked away until you leave.
• the **Steuerrechnung**, which comes as a bill in the following year and is not taken off your wage.
• the **Prämie**, which goes up every January.

And the thing worth knowing before you lie awake over it: **you can pay in Raten.** Call and ask. The answer is yes, it is completely ordinary, and the call takes four minutes.

title: halt and eben, and the shrug inside them
text:
Two words that mean nothing and change everything. They sit in the middle of the sentence, after the verb, where you can miss them for two years.

**halt** — that is how it is, and nothing can change it.

• Das ist **halt** so.
• Dann gehen wir **halt** später.
• Er ist **halt** so.

There is a small shrug inside every one of them. It is not giving up: giving up means you wanted something and stopped. Halt means it was never going to change and you are carrying on anyway.

**eben** — yes, exactly, that is the point.

Agreement without enthusiasm, which is the local default. Two men can hold an entire negotiation with six of them. **Eben drum** is the longer form and it means *for exactly that reason* — the politest way there is of telling somebody they are being slow.

**Both of them close a topic.** Halt closes it because nothing can be done; eben closes it because everybody agrees. Whoever keeps talking afterwards has missed something.

**And there is one place halt does not go.** A train, a bill, some rain: halt. A death: never. Saying it about something big makes the thing smaller than it is, and everybody hears that at once.

title: doch, which English has no word for
text:
Somebody says something negative. You disagree. In English you have to build a sentence. Here you say one word.

• Du hast nicht angerufen. — **Doch.**
• Das stimmt nicht. — **Doch.**
• Du magst kein Fondue. — **Doch.**

**Ja does not work there.** If somebody says you did not call and you answer ja, you have just agreed with them. That is the mistake everybody makes, for about two years, and nobody will correct it — they will simply ask the question again a different way.

**doch, doch** is the soft version: *it is fine, stop apologising.* You will hear it every time you say sorry for something small.

In the middle of a sentence it stops being an answer and becomes a tone:

• **Komm doch mit** — an invitation, where *komm mit* is an instruction.
• **Das habe ich dir doch gesagt** — a reproach, said calmly. Careful with this one. It means *you were not listening*, and some people say it to each other for forty years.

And at the front of a question it is a reminder rather than a question: *Du kommst doch am Samstag?* The only answer to that is yes.

title: Everything asked of you has a mal in it
text:
A bare imperative is grammatically perfect and too hard for this country. *Komm. Warte. Schau.* You will hear those with children, with dogs and in the army. With adults there is a **mal** in the middle.

• Schau **mal**. Sag **mal**. Warte **mal**. Komm **mal** her.

Mal means nothing at all. What it does is make the thing small, so the other person can say yes easily. **kurz** is the second softener and does the same job: *Hast du kurz Zeit?* Kurz is usually a lie and everybody knows it — it is a form, not a claim.

Two softeners is the ceiling. *Könntest du mal kurz schauen?* is normal. Add a third and it stops sounding polite and starts sounding like somebody hiding something, and here that is worse.

**eigentlich** belongs to this family and it is a warning light. On its own it is fine: *Eigentlich wollte ich früher gehen.* But **eigentlich schon** is a no. It means: that works in theory and we are not doing it. Ask once, plainly, whether it is a yes — asking twice stops being about the thing and starts being about whether the other person is honest.

title: Nicht schlecht is the top of the scale
text:
Praise here is a currency and it is kept scarce. The whole scale is shifted downwards, and you have to see all of it once:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Geht so** | it is bad |
| **Ganz gut** | it is mediocre |
| **Gut** | it is good |
| **Nicht schlecht** | it is very good |
| **Sehr gut** | an event, from an adult |

**Ganz gut is the trap.** *Ganz* makes the word weaker, not stronger. And there is a level above all of it with no words in it at all: somebody eats and says nothing and takes seconds.

It runs the same way downwards. Nothing is a catastrophe. *Nicht so gut*, *eher schwierig*, *da hat es noch Luft* — all three mean do it again.

The third rule is about you. **You do not accept praise.** Somebody says you cook well and you say *ach was*, or *das kann jeder*, and then they say it again. It is a dance and both sides know the steps. Saying only thank you breaks it off — not a disaster, and it is noticed.

And do not overdo it in the other direction either. If everything is fantastic, nothing is.

title: They only tease people they have decided about
text:
Somebody tells you something ridiculous, with a completely flat face, and lets you believe it for four minutes. **The four minutes are the joke.**

• **Jemand nimmt dich auf den Arm.** — somebody is having you on.
• **Das war doch nur ein Spass.**

The hard part is not the words. It is that here a joke carries **no signal**: no raised eyebrows, no change of voice, no pause. The sentence arrives at the same volume as a sentence about the recycling, and the person is looking at their glass while they say it.

There are two reasons for that, and the second one is the good one. A joke with packaging shows off a little. And without a signal, whoever notices belongs, and whoever does not loses nothing, because they noticed nothing. **Nobody is embarrassed in either direction.**

The thing that looks like mockery from outside is the opposite. **They do not do it to a guest.** It is a statement that you belong, said with a made-up story instead of with the words.

Two sentences worth having: **Jetzt nimmst du mich auf den Arm** and **Das glaube ich dir nicht.** The second one is your best defence and about half the time you will be wrong, because the story was true.

title: Complaining is a greeting, not a topic
text:
There are two completely different things with the same name.

**The real one.** *Ich möchte eine Rechnung reklamieren.* Calm, precise, with the number to hand. Nobody has to be convinced; either you are right or you are not, and both are clear in four minutes. It is far less frightening than it looks, and the fear costs more than the call.

**The other one** is a social form and it has three subjects: the trains, the prices, and Zurich. You can have it with anybody in the country.

• **Das ist doch nicht möglich.**
• **Das kann ja nicht sein.**
• **Und das bei diesen Preisen.**

Its rules: it is **never serious** — a country where the trains run to the minute is exactly the country that complains about four of them. You do not complain *to* somebody, you complain *with* them, so contradicting is a failure to understand the game. And it lasts about two minutes. Somebody still on the train after four is unpleasant.

It is the local weather conversation with more opinion in it, and in a place where people do not talk much, two minutes of agreeing with a stranger is an offer.

title: Six days, and a valve with a date on it
text:
It starts at **five in the morning**, in the dark, in February, on Schmutziger Donnerstag. That moment is the **Urknall**: one bang, all the lights, and twenty bands at once out of every lane. Not one after another. Together.

The words:

• **die Gugge** — a brass band that plays deliberately wrong, and rehearses all winter to play it wrong the same way every time.
• **die Grinde** — the mask, in Luzern. Basel says Larve.
• **d'Räppli** — confetti, from Rappen, because they look like little coins. You will find them in a jacket in July.
• **das Sujet** — the theme a band takes for the year, and twenty-five identical costumes sewn in the autumn.

It is officially six days and everybody says three. Sleep is not part of it. It ends on Tuesday at three in the morning, **in the middle of a piece**, and by nine on Ash Wednesday the town is clean and everybody is at work.

**That is the point of it.** In a country that is precise all year, this is a valve, and the valve has a date on it. Behind a mask nobody can hear where you are from — which is the best and the saddest thing about the whole week.

title: An opinion, put down loosely
text:
Say *das ist falsch* flatly to a table here and you will watch the table move. The problem is not the opinion — everybody probably agreed. The problem is the form.

An opinion is not put down flat. It is put down and left slightly open:

• **Ich finde eigentlich** …
• **Mir scheint** …
• **Ich habe den Eindruck** …
• **Für mich ist es so, dass** …

All four say *this is mine*. They do not say *this is how it is*. Whoever says how it is has decided for everybody; whoever says how they find it has only spoken for themselves, and then other people can add something without a fight.

This is not timidity, and it took me a year to stop reading it that way. People say a great deal and they say it very directly. They just do not say it as the last word. **A conversation is a table everybody puts something on**, not a competition somebody wins. The country is governed the same way, and it is why seven ministers from four parties all say the same thing on a Wednesday.

The sentence that carries the whole principle is four words: **Ich sehe das anders.** Very calm, and it attacks nobody and gives up nothing.

title: The envelope on the kitchen table
text:
Four times a year a **Couvert** lands on every kitchen table in the country. Inside are the ballot papers and a booklet of about forty pages explaining both sides, soberly. Nobody reads all of it.

• **abstimmen** — to decide about a thing.
• **wählen** — to send people into an office.

Those are not the same and they are easy to confuse. Things are voted on here far more often than people. An **Initiative** is a proposal from the public: a hundred thousand signatures and it goes to a vote. That is why there are people with clipboards outside every larger shop.

• **Ich bin dafür.** **Ich bin dagegen.** **Ich weiss noch nicht.**

The third one is completely normal and nobody pushes.

**Two things nobody tells you.** You do not ask how somebody voted — if they want to say, they say. And on Monday it is over: a result decided by one per cent is a state of affairs by Tuesday and not a subject. *Das Volk hat entschieden*, said calmly, including by the people who lost. That acceptance is the actual machine, more than the voting is.

About a quarter of the adults here may not vote at all. That is worth knowing before you admire the system too loudly.

title: Two steps back instead of one
text:
You have been telling the past with **hat** and **ist** since phase 2, and it has been enough. There is one place it is not.

When you are already in the past and want to go further back, you take **hatte** or **war** and put the verb at the end.

• Ich **hatte** das nicht gewusst.
• Sie **war** schon gegangen, als ich gekommen bin.
• Er **hatte** den Brief zweimal gelesen.

That is the whole tense. It has a long name and it is the easiest thing in this phase.

The words around it matter more than the form:

• **seit** — from then until now. *Ich wohne seit fünf Jahren hier.*
• **vor** — a point in the past. *Vor fünf Jahren bin ich gekommen.*
• **inzwischen** — the road between the two, and it carries a change with it. *Inzwischen kenne ich die Namen von den Bergen.*

**inzwischen** is the one worth having. It says: it was one way, time passed, and now it is another way — in a single word, without your having to say any of that.

title: ohne nachzudenken
text:
A small piece of machinery that you will use for the rest of your life here.

**ohne** plus **zu** plus the verb at the end:

• Ich habe es gesagt, **ohne nachzudenken**.
• Er ist gegangen, **ohne** etwas **zu sagen**.

And with a separable verb the **zu** goes into the middle of the word:

• nach**zu**denken
• auf**zu**stehen
• an**zu**rufen

That is the one part you have to memorise, because you cannot hear it.

The same shape works with **um** for a purpose and **statt** for an alternative: *Ich bin gekommen, um zu helfen.* *Statt zu fragen, hat er es selber gemacht.*

Three small words, one **zu**, and the verb at the end. It is worth more than it looks: it is what lets one sentence carry two ideas without a **dass** in it, and that is how people actually talk.

title: An deiner Stelle würde ich
text:
Advice, without telling anybody what to do.

• **An deiner Stelle würde ich** das nehmen.
• **An deiner Stelle würde ich** noch warten.

You do not say *nimm das*. You do not say *das ist besser*. You stand next to the person and look at the thing with them, and the form says so.

Everything else runs on **würde** plus the verb at the end:

• Ich **würde** sagen, das reicht.
• Ich **würde** eher warten.
• Das **würde** ich nicht machen.

That last one is a very clear warning and it sounds like nothing at all. If somebody says it to you, stop.

**Two more that do the same job:**

• **Ich habe den Eindruck, dass** … — I have the impression that.
• **Vielleicht wäre es besser, wenn** … — maybe it would be better if.

They are all longer than the sentence they replace. That is the point: the length is the politeness, and here it is worth what it costs.

title: Explaining it to somebody newer than you
text:
One day somebody will ask you where the rubbish goes, and this is the whole of what to do about it.

**Answer the question that was asked.** They asked one thing. Your first year is not the answer, however much you want to tell it. Four boxes, four words, and the exceptions in the second year when they need them.

**Say ganz einfach only when it is.** *Ganz einfach, schau* followed by four exceptions is a lie, and it teaches somebody that they are stupid.

**nochmal** is short for noch einmal and everybody says the short form. Use it without making it a favour: *Ich sage es nochmal*, and then just say it again.

**Do not slow down for them.** The people who help most talk at their normal speed and take you with them. The difference between helping and belittling is not in the language, it is in the face — whoever slows down and waits has made the other person small.

And if you share another language with them, decide once, out loud, and then stop deciding: *Wollen wir Deutsch reden? Ich wechsle, wenn es nicht mehr geht.* You will find out how hard that is the first time you are the one who could switch.

title: When they stop switching
text:
This is the last thing in the course and it is the one nobody warns you about.

You are talking German. You pause for half a second looking for a word. Somebody says the word in English, kindly, to help — and the whole table carries on in English for two minutes.

Nobody does that unkindly. **Everybody does it, and they do it because they can.** A country where almost everybody speaks good English is the hardest possible place to learn its language, and that is not a complaint, it is just the arithmetic.

What helps:

• **Sag es einfach anders.** Say it another way. Four sentences instead of one is a win, not a failure.
• Ask for the German word in German: **Wie sagt man, wenn** …
• And say it once, plainly, to the people you see most: *Red mit mir Deutsch, auch wenn es länger dauert.*

There is no exam here and no letter and nobody congratulates you. There is only an evening, years in, when you notice afterwards that nobody changed language for you all night.

**Do not say it out loud at the table.** Everybody would say something kind, and then next time they would be watching for it again. Some things only work as long as nobody names them.
